Extraction: From Manual to Agentic Security Operations: A Multi-Dimensional Evaluation of AI-Driven SOC Architectures (title page, p. 1).

Mutaz Abdel Wahed (Faculty of Information Technology, Jadara University, Irbid, Jordan; corresponding author) and Nader Mohammad Aljawarneh (School of Business, Jadara University, Irbid, Jordan) (p. 1).

2026 — Journal of Information & Knowledge Management (World Scientific), Vol. 25, No. 9, art. 2650039 (27 pages), DOI 10.1142/S0219649226500395; received 23 Jan 2026, accepted 1 Mar 2026, published 22 Jun 2026 (p. 1).

Security Operations Centres (SOCs) face rising alert volumes, analyst overload and fatigue, delayed incident response and inconsistent decision quality, with most alerts being false alarms that still require manual analysis (Abstract, p. 1; §1, p. 2). SOAR-based automation remains reactive, rule/script-driven and dependent on human judgment, so it does not solve the scalability and cognitive limits of analyst-centric SOCs (§1, p. 2; §2, p. 4). In parallel, academic literature lacks a rigorous framework to evaluate the operational impact of autonomous/AI-driven SOCs: existing maturity and benchmarking models focus on tooling and process and ignore decision autonomy, decision quality and analyst experience, and often fail to distinguish scripted automation from true agentic autonomy (§1, pp. 2-3; §2, p. 5).

The paper proposes (i) the 3E multi-dimensional evaluation framework — Efficiency (detection/response latency), Effectiveness (false-positive reduction, remediation success) and Experience (analyst workload and decision oversight) — mapped to RQ1-RQ4 (§3, p. 6; Table 1 and Fig. 2, p. 7), and (ii) an agentic SOC architecture in which AI agents autonomously ingest, enrich, cluster, prioritise and remediate alerts under 'bounded autonomy' with humans kept at strategic checkpoints for high-severity or ambiguous incidents (§3, p. 10; Fig. 3, p. 11; §4, p. 17). The architecture is layered — perception (SIEM/EDR/network telemetry), reasoning (rule-based logic plus probabilistic classifiers), orchestration (autonomous actions, escalation, human-in-the-loop interventions) and execution with a feedback learning loop (§3, p. 10) — and implements a multi-tier remediation hierarchy (Network, Endpoint, Identity, System Integrity controls; Table 6, p. 15). Agentic AI's role is thus autonomous Tier-1 triage/pre-classification and confidence-scored remediation, shifting analysts to supervisory governance (§3, p. 8; §4, pp. 15-16).

Comparative operational evaluation (simulation study) contrasting two SOC scenarios — a traditional analyst-centric SIEM/manual-triage workflow versus an agentic AI-enhanced workflow — over a 90-day simulated observation window using synthetic but empirically grounded security telemetry calibrated on SOC benchmarking research and industry surveys (alert frequency, severity distribution, escalation patterns), since production telemetry is sensitive and no public end-to-end datasets exist (§3, pp. 6, 8). Both scenarios share identical alert sources, distributions and observation windows for internal validity (§3, pp. 6, 10). Quantitative metrics are formally defined: MTTD, MTTR, False Positive Ratio, Escalation Rate and Automation Impact (§3, p. 12); analysis uses descriptive statistics and effect-oriented percentage comparisons, explicitly avoiding hypothesis testing for the operational contrast (§3, p. 10). Complementarily, PLS-SEM over 5,571 alert-level observations tests four latent constructs (analyst efficiency, alert complexity, automation impact, decision quality) with composite reliability >0.70 and AVE >0.50 (§3, p. 11; Table 8, p. 20), and a confusion matrix (N=5,571) yields precision 0.873, recall 0.929, F1 0.900, accuracy 0.951 (§4, p. 22; Fig. 10). The Experience dimension uses system-based proxies (intervention frequency, override rates, reassignments) — no direct analyst survey was carried out (§3, pp. 6, 10).

Central metrics, empirically compared against a concrete baseline (the traditional analyst-centric SOC workflow) — but both arms run on synthetic/simulated 90-day telemetry, not production data, so gains are comparative-in-simulation (§3, p. 8). Headline results: MTTD fell from 6-12 h (traditional) to 30-90 min (agentic) and MTTR from 12-24 h to 2-6 h, reported as 75% and 80% improvements (§4, p. 13; Table 3, p. 14), with markedly lower MTTR variance and tail latency (Fig. 4, p. 13). A second summary table reports different magnitudes/units — MTTD 18.2 min -> 10.2 min (44%) and MTTR 32.5 min -> 17.2 min (47%) (Table 9, p. 20) — an internal inconsistency with Table 3; the text also cites 34-47% improvement in time-based efficiency measures (§4, p. 19). In a simulated zero-day scenario, total response/containment time dropped from 42 min to 9 min (76% reduction; Table 10, pp. 20-21).

Field: General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Agent Systems
Extraction: Conceptually, the paper sharpens the distinction between rule-based/scripted automation (SOAR) and agentic autonomy — goal-directed behaviour, contextual reasoning, dynamic action selection and outcome-based strategy adaptation (§1, p. 3; §2, p. 5). It contributes a governance model of 'bounded autonomy': autonomy delivers the largest gains in high-volume, low-context routine alert handling, while high-severity, ambiguous, business-impacting incidents still require human judgment at strategic checkpoints (§4, p. 17; §5, p. 24). It evidences a structural redistribution of knowledge work — analysts move from execution to supervision, auditing and exception handling, requiring new AI-oversight skills (§4, pp. 15-16; §5, p. 24) — and frames agentic SOCs as socio-technical, knowledge-intensive systems from an IKM perspective (§1, p. 3; §6, p. 26). It is a single agentic overlay with tiered autonomous remediation actions rather than an explicit multi-agent LLM system; implementation details of the agents (models, algorithms) are not specified (§3, pp. 10-11).

Authors acknowledge external-validity constraints of synthetic telemetry: it cannot reproduce the ambiguity of novel attacks requiring human intuition, and the simulation omits organisational factors such as team dynamics and communication overhead (§3, p. 8). The Experience dimension relies on system-based proxies and modelled interactions — no direct analyst survey — so subjective perceptions (trust, fatigue) are not directly captured and some experience indicators are themselves simulated (§3, pp. 6, 10; §4, p. 19). Additional observed weaknesses: MTTD/MTTR baselines differ in scale between Table 3 (hours; p. 14) and Table 9 (minutes; p. 20) without reconciliation, and the agentic system's implementation (algorithms, models, LLM usage) is not described in reproducible detail (§3, pp. 10-11). Adoption barriers identified: fragmented telemetry, legacy data formats, distrust of AI decisions and organisational reluctance to delegate authority (§5, p. 25). Future work: integrating explainable AI mechanisms, longitudinal real-world deployments and refined human-control/governance mechanisms (§6, p. 26).

Directly relevant: the study quantifies (in simulation) how agentic AI reduces MTTD and MTTR in SOC incident response against an analyst-centric baseline — exactly the thesis's dependent variables — and its 'bounded autonomy' human-in-the-loop model (§4, p. 17; Fig. 3, p. 11) is adjacent to the agentic-copilot paradigm in which the human retains decision authority. The 3E framework (Efficiency/Effectiveness/Experience) and its RQ-to-metric mapping (Table 1, p. 7) offer a reusable evaluation template for the dissertation's measurement design, and the triage-bottleneck evidence (FPR 0.544 in manual triage; Table 5, p. 14) supports the copilot-value argument. Evidential weight is tempered by the synthetic nature of the telemetry and by internal metric inconsistencies (Tables 3 vs. 9). The study enters the corpus with the mandatory stratum caveat (Qualis A3 — PDR-0007).

High — it is one of the few studies that empirically compares traditional vs. agentic SOC workflows with MTTD/MTTR as primary endpoints (Tables 3, 9, 10) and proposes an evaluation framework directly reusable by the thesis. The score reflects thematic centrality; evidence strength is moderated by the synthetic/simulated data and the Qualis A3 stratum caveat (PDR-0007).
